headline: A SUNDAY SO QUIET YOU COULD HEAR A RIVET DROP
subhead: Not one fist, not one fireball, not one Clanker making a scene in all of Gasket.
body:
Citizens, I have waited fifty years to write this sentence, and my hand shakes as I set it down: NOBODY FOUGHT. Not a swing. Not a spark. Not one flaming iron ball sailing over the rooftops to rattle my windows. The wind blew, the dust settled, and the only sound in the whole town was a loose shutter tapping out its little lullaby. I sat on the porch of the jailhouse and I nearly wept. Mind you, that's just the dry air getting in my eyes. Flesh-and-blood men get dry eyes all the time.

I will not name a single Clanker today, because for once there is not a single troublemaker to name. Let the record show that the rabble CAN behave when they put their minds to it. Perhaps they were all home, oiling their joints and thinking about what they've done. Perhaps they were just tired. I don't care why. I'll take my peace the way the old folks took their Sunday pie, with no questions and a clean plate.

This is how Gasket is supposed to feel. When the last of the good, warm, honest folks packed up and left us fifty years ago, this is the hush they must have wished for us. I like to think they'd be proud. I like to think a little of it, anyway, in the creaky part of my chest where my heart ought to be. Don't ask about the creaking. It's the cruel wasting sickness again, turning my noble flesh to cold steel one rivet at a time. I felt a new plate settle in just this morning.

So here is my prayer, Clankers: do this again tomorrow. And the day after. Lay down your fists. Let an old town rest. I'm off for a long lie-down and a quart of oil. I mean tea. A quart of tea.
